title: Type Conversion and Coercion
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of type conversion and coercion in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply type conversion and coercion in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to handling invalid conversions and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Type Conversion and Coercion through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding type conversion and coercion helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Type Conversion and Coercion helps you reason about converting strings and numbers. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Converting strings and numbers. Then connect it to to_i , to_f , to_s , and to_sym. The remaining syllabus points—Explicit versus implicit conversions, Handling invalid conversions—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports type conversion and coercion. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for type conversion and coercion using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Handling invalid conversions), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Run, troubleshoot, and reset
content_blocks.text: Save as lesson.rb and run `ruby lesson.rb` from a terminal. CodeLeaf currently has no isolated Ruby runner, so these examples should be run locally until one is deployed. If the command fails, confirm `ruby --version`, inspect the full error message, and verify that required standard-library or gem dependencies are installed. Reset by removing temporary files created by your experiment and returning the code to the smallest reproducible example.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain type conversion and coercion, identify its place in data types, literals, and operators, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
